transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (NovusHealth - Lead ML Eng), Aisha Khan (PM), Tom Becker (Infra), Priyanka (QA)

Summary:
Quick sync on week-2 POC cache metrics. We reviewed prefix + KV cache hit rate, prompt reuse patterns, emergent token savings, and a small tuning pass that bumped hit-rate on mid-frequency flows. Agreed next steps: share dashboard and config snippets, run 48h throughput test in staging, validate eviction policy and confirm GPU provisioning.

Topics:
- Raw KV hit-rate breakdown by route
- Prompt grouping / canonicalization strategy to increase prefix reuse
- Latency vs cold-start cost tradeoffs with larger caching windows
- Eviction policy and memory pressure during spikes
- Security/compliance notes re: data retention and KMS keys

Action items (captured here as well): Jordan to send exports; Maya to share grouping rules; Carlos/Tom to run infra test.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, uh, Maya and I are from Redwood, and then from Novus?
[00:06] Carlos Rivera: Carlos here, hi.
[00:07] Aisha Khan: Aisha on product.
[00:08] Tom Becker: Tom for infra.
[00:09] Priyanka: Priyanka QA.
[00:11] Jordan Lee: Awesome. We have about 55 minutes, agenda is a short review of the dashboard, then tuning notes, then agree next steps. Maya will take us through the numbers.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Okay, jump in. So this is the pilot dashboard link (https://redwood.app/links/novus/pilot-dashboard) — I dropped the CSV export in the drive as well. The headline: overall KV hit-rate is 41% across all routes; prefix cache hit-rate for the conversational route is 62% after the grouping pass we ran last Thursday.
[00:44] Carlos Rivera: Wait, 62? I thought we were seeing high mid-40s for that route in staging. Did you include the prompt canonicalization step?
[00:50] Maya Chen: Yes, we applied the canonicalization and merged paraphrases into three buckets for the top 20 intents. That reduced token variance and improved prefix matching. There is a caveat — the improvement is concentrated in mid-frequency requests, the tail of rare prompts stayed low.
[01:10] Aisha Khan: Can you explain the paraphrase merge? Like are you rewriting customer prompts? I want to make sure product owners know we're not changing user's wording.
[01:18] Maya Chen: Good call. It's not user-facing rewrite. It's an internal preprocessing canonicalizer that normalizes system instructions and common phrasings. So the model sees more consistent prefixes. We log the originals and you can opt out per route.
[01:34] Tom Becker: How does that affect privacy? Are originals stored in the cache? Our compliance folks asked if anything PII gets materialized in Redis/K-V store.
[01:44] Jordan Lee: Short answer: no raw PII is persistently stored in plaintext. Redwood's default is to hash keys and we can enable KMS-backed envelope encryption. We also have per-tenant TTLs; the pilot used a 7-day default but we can adjust to your retention policy. We'll attach the SOC2/security brief.
[02:05] Carlos Rivera: Ok that's helpful. On the hit-rate CSV I saw there was a column labeled 'k-v cash' — that's a transcription typo in the export?
[02:12] Maya Chen: Yeah, that's my bad — legacy naming, we call it k_v_cash in the export schema, sorry.
[02:20] Priyanka: There's some noise in the logs during spike test 2 where we saw evictions. Can you share eviction policy config? It looked like LRU but maybe we didn't set weights correctly.
[02:30] Maya Chen: For the pilot we used an LRU with a size limit per pool. We recommended a weighted-LRU for conversational sessions so session-start prefixes are favored. I can share the snippet.
[02:39] Jordan Lee: The important metric here is hit-rate at the router-level, but also the cost-savings per 100k requests. We estimated token reduction by ~17% on mid-frequency flows which translates to roughly 23% compute savings on that route in dedicated capacity.
[02:56] Carlos Rivera: That estimate assumed consistent KV warmers; what about cold-starts in the morning when traffic ramps? We saw 10-15% degraded latency on the first half-hour.
[03:07] Maya Chen: Right—cold start penalty is real. We recommend a small background pre-warm job that walks the hot keys at off-peak times, and optionally a tiny on-prem warm cache to reduce cross-region fetches. For the staging ramp we did a 30-minute pre-warm and latency tail improved by ~120ms.
[03:26] Tom Becker: Pre-warm is fine but that requires extra GPU time — we're sensitive to cost. Can we accept slightly higher latency? The SLA target is 250ms p95; current p95 for the route is 310ms when cold.
[03:37] Jordan Lee: Trade-off depends on which SLO you want to prioritize. You can tighten the prefix canonicalization and increase cache TTL to reduce cold misses, or run scheduled pre-warms. We'll show two config options in the snippet: cost-optimized and latency-optimized.
[03:50] Aisha Khan: For product, the main success criteria is user-facing latency <300ms and no regression in quality. How do we ensure canonicalization doesn't degrade output quality?
[03:59] Maya Chen: We ran an eval set of 500 prompts and measured BLEU-ish similarity and response acceptance. Canonicalization slightly changed tokens but model outputs stayed within your QA thresholds. We'll attach the eval pack (link: drive/novus/canonical-evals).
[04:14] Carlos Rivera: One weird thing — for one intent the hit-rate dropped after canonicalization. I dug in: the paraphrase bucketing collapsed two prompts that had subtle context differences, so the cached prefix returned an answer with the wrong persona.
[04:26] Maya Chen: Good catch — that's exactly why we include a human-in-the-loop review for bucket mappings. For those ambiguous pairs we mark them as 'do not merge'. The re-run bumped that intent back to previous accuracy but lowered hit-rate slightly for that bucket. It's a precision/recall style tradeoff.
[04:44] Priyanka: QA found a flake where the KV key hashing collided for long prefixes. Is that possible?
[04:50] Maya Chen: Collisions are extremely unlikely — we use SHA-256 and namespace salts per-tenant. But if you truncated hashes in your local export it might look colliding. We'll share the hashing spec.
[05:02] Jordan Lee: Let's talk about the grouping strategy. Maya, walk through the three-tier grouping you recommended.
[05:07] Maya Chen: Sure. Tier 1: verbatim session identifiers — exact match for high-frequency customer flows. Tier 2: paraphrase buckets for top 20 intents — use sentence embeddings + clustering with a manual review pass. Tier 3: generic system instruction normalization for everything else. We also add a small heuristic: retain first N tokens of user utterance for context to avoid over-generalization.
[05:31] Carlos Rivera: For clustering, what's the threshold? We don't want to under- or over-cluster.
[05:35] Maya Chen: We used a cosine threshold of 0.78 with manual spot checks; the config is tunable and we'll put that value in the config snippet.
[05:44] Aisha Khan: Any notes on multi-turn KV caching? We noticed that sometimes earlier turns bleed into later answers because the prefix included session metadata.
[05:52] Maya Chen: We recommend isolating session-local KV entries from global prefix entries. Keep session KV TTL short and avoid caching system-level state. For generative reuse, cache only the system + user prompt prefix that leads to the model continuation, not the entire conversation.
[06:10] Tom Becker: About eviction — when memory pressure hits, what should we do? Increase swap? Add nodes? Change policy?
[06:16] Maya Chen: First quick fix is increase per-pool size or LRU weights for session-pref keys. Medium fix: add an extra cache node or increase memory per node. Long-term: use a tiered cache with a hot in-memory layer and a warm SSD-backed layer; Redwood Dedicated supports that topology.
[06:33] Jordan Lee: For the 48-hour run we suggested: run with canonicalization + tiered prefix grouping on 50% of traffic, keep 50% as baseline. That gives an A/B to measure both hit-rate and quality regression.
[06:47] Carlos Rivera: Sounds good. We'll need the config snippet and a small script to split traffic. Also need to make sure the experiment is visible in our observability stack.
[06:55] Maya Chen: We'll provide an nginx style split example and the route-level flags you can flip. We'll also add tracing headers for span correlation.
[07:05] Aisha Khan: On security, Tom asked about KMS. We need BYOK and audit logs for cache writes.
[07:12] Jordan Lee: Redwood supports BYOK for cache encryption and audit logs. We'll attach docs and a short runbook for rotating keys.
[07:20] Tom Becker: For the 48h test, I'll need 4 extra GPUs for the dedicated pool — can Redwood confirm capacity?
[07:27] Jordan Lee: We have capacity in the target region; I'll confirm after this call and add it to the ticket.
[07:33] Maya Chen: Quick note: pipeline-level batching can interact with caching. If you increase max-batch-size you may increase cache reuse because similar requests sit in the same micro-batch, but it can also increase latency. We'll add recommended batching config.
[07:50] Carlos Rivera: Can you share the raw per-route CSV one more time? I want to run my own pivot tables.
[07:55] Jordan Lee: Yep — dropping link in chat now: https://redwood.app/links/novus/pilot-csv (also in drive).
[08:02] Priyanka: QA will pull the eval set and re-run acceptance tests during the 48h. Expect us to flag any output-quality regressions within 72 hours.
[08:10] Maya Chen: Great. I'll also add a small smoke test that runs after each deploy to validate cache integrity.
[08:16] Jordan Lee: Final recap — action items: Jordan will send the export and security brief; Maya will send grouping config, canonicalization rules, and sampling evals; Carlos/Tom will run the 48h test and provision infra; Priyanka will run QA acceptance. We'll meet again after the 48h window.
[08:33] Carlos Rivera: Thanks, appreciate the clear steps.
[08:35] Aisha Khan: Thanks everyone.
[08:37] Jordan Lee: Bye all.

End of transcript.
